History:
- Main complaint: Progressive swelling of the upper lip, onset after eating prawn soup.
- Onset: Approximately 30 minutes after ingestion; currently ongoing and worsening.
- Progression: Lip swelling began at the left corner and spread; swelling is increasing; sensation of “pumping blood”; associated with difficulty breathing and possible throat tightness.
- Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath, feeling dizzy.
- Similar episode: About one year ago after eating out (food possibly curry), woke up with swollen lip and difficulty breathing.
- Context: Patient has a known peanut allergy.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (regular use of salbutamol inhaler).
- Peanut allergy (history of previous hospitalization/severe reaction as a child requiring injection—exact treatment not specified).
- Previous episode of food-associated angioedema with respiratory symptoms.
- Medications: Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented); antihistamines used occasionally (name/dose not documented).
- Allergies: Peanut allergy (confirmed); prawn allergy not previously documented but suspected.

Physical Examination:
- Reported upper lip swelling, worsening.
- Feeling of throat tightness/difficulty breathing.
- Reports dizziness during the consultation.
- No documentation of throat swelling or rash.
- No mention of other physical findings.
- Patient was alert and able to answer questions.

Impression:
- Suspected anaphylactic reaction following exposure to prawn soup.

Management Plan:
- Strongly advised immediate ambulance call to emergency services (999) due to signs of anaphylaxis.
- Advised to take available antihistamines while waiting for emergency assistance.
- Ensure presence of another person (mother now with patient) for safety and to assist.
- Advised to follow up after hospital discharge to consider provision of emergency injection (e.g., epinephrine auto-injector).

Patient Summary:
- Patient with asthma and peanut allergy developed rapid-onset lip swelling and respiratory symptoms after eating prawn soup; this is suspected to be an anaphylactic reaction.
- Emergency services were called; antihistamines advised while awaiting help.
- Plan includes acute hospital care and follow-up for further allergy management.

Key Takeaways:
- Seek immediate help and call emergency services when experiencing lip swelling and difficulty breathing after eating.
- Take antihistamines promptly if available during allergic reactions, but still seek emergency care.
- Follow up with healthcare provider after discharge for long-term allergy and anaphylaxis management.

Next Steps:
- Immediate ambulance transport and emergency care.
- In-hospital assessment and treatment of suspected anaphylaxis.
- Follow-up appointment after hospital discharge to discuss ongoing allergy management and possible prescription of epinephrine auto-injector.

Quality checks:

- Missing elements: No documentation of medication doses, routes, or frequency (except for salbutamol inhaler, which also lacks detail). No full review of systems, no exact physical examination or vital signs. No documentation of any comorbidities beyond asthma and allergies.
- No major internal conflicts detected; all history appears consistent.
- Transcript quality: Clear, minimal irrelevant dialogue, all clinically pertinent details captured.
